centralObject.name: Judge Jamal Whitehead's temporary restraining order of 2026-11-05 (W.D. Wash., OneAmerica Votes v. Trump, No. 2:26-cv-04223-JNW), barring DOJ and DHS for 14 days from directing Washington election officials to remove, withhold or set aside the ballots of specific voters in the 2026-11-03 election, or threatening them with prosecution for refusing

place.why: The order stops DOJ from compelling Washington to set ballots aside through the November 24 county certification, but it lasts 14 days, the injunction hearing is November 18, and investigations can go ahead, so it delivers on the count without settling the citizenship question.

tethers.title: Federal crime for a noncitizen to vote in a federal election
tethers.why: The only authority DOJ's October 26 letter cited (order at 6). Whitehead, following the Ninth Circuit's October 30 ruling in United States v. California, held it does not let DOJ take charge of a state's running election; prosecutions under it remain open. Enactment date carried from the California draft (rdg_al8uju97ware), not re-verified.

place.why: As DOJ's lever on the count it failed here; it stands only as the route to case-by-case prosecution after the fact.

tethers.title: States prescribe the times, places and manner of congressional elections; Congress may alter those regulations
tethers.why: The ground of the likely-success finding: DOJ exceeded the authority Congress has delegated under the Clause, with Printz's anti-commandeering line (order at 16-19). Ratification date from background.

place.why: Leaves the count to the procedures Washington's legislature enacted unless Congress itself says otherwise.

tethers.title: NVRA 90-day bar on systematic removals before a federal election
tethers.why: Cited through the Ninth Circuit's California ruling (order at 17): the demand likely conflicts with the 90-day bar. Not the ground Whitehead rested on. Section and date from the California draft.

place.why: Standing law that runs against list-based pulls this close to an election; in the background here.

tethers.title: SAVE Act
tethers.statusAsOf: Passed House 2025-04-10; received in the Senate, no vote (catalog)
tethers.why: Documentary proof of citizenship at registration: the front-end check B-fluid and D-coalition name as the right fix instead of pulling ballots after the vote.

place.why: Stalled in the Senate, so it delivers nothing to this count; it is the answer the right names for next time.

title: Did Not Ask
prompt: A judge told federal prosecutors they can't make Washington set aside ballots from a list of suspected noncitizens. Is that the states running their own count, or a court shielding illegal votes?
framing: On Thursday, November 5, 2026, U.S. District Judge Jamal Whitehead in Seattle issued a 14-day temporary restraining order barring the Justice Department and Homeland Security from directing Washington election officials to drop specific voters from the rolls, withhold their ballots, or set aside their votes in the November 3 election, and from threatening officials with prosecution for refusing. On October 26, federal prosecutors had sent Secretary of State Steve Hobbs a list of roughly 400 registered voters they suspected were noncitizens, citing only 18 U.S.C. § 611 and giving no individual evidence, and asked that those ballots not be counted until citizenship was settled. Hobbs refused on October 28, saying the list included citizens. Whitehead found the challengers likely to win on the claim that DOJ exceeded its authority under the Elections Clause. Investigations and prosecutions can continue.

split.seam: At the center it is a 3-vs-1 peel: A (+0.75), C (+0.6) and B (+0.3) read the order as delivering on fluid, D alone negative (−0.6). At the rim it closes into an x split: B (−0.7) and C (−0.5) cross negative, only A's rim (+0.8) stays positive.
split.rationale: At the center Printz and the Elections Clause do the sorting, and a right-institutional speaker who reads them as federalism accepts the order. At the rim the holder takes over: a Biden judge and the Elias lawyers for the right, a court that leaves the list in DOJ's hands for C.

zPattern.note: Centers are fluid z; coalition z: A +0.5, B −0.1, C +0.3, D −0.35. B and C change sign between fluid and denominated; B already crosses at coalition. Object z +0.5.

antiValentRationale: The coalition band is where each station turns on its own side: A tells the people celebrating that a TRO isn't a verdict, B defends the judge's Printz reasoning against people calling him a Biden judge, C won't cheer a D.C. law firm while the list stays in DOJ's hands, and D tells the people yelling rigged that the list was sloppy and DOJ handed the judge the case.

z.pos: the order delivers: a state's count runs on its own rules, and a federal list with no evidence can't pull ballots out of it
z.neg: it doesn't: a judge shields suspect votes from the one check that might have caught them, two days after the election

fluid.zReason: Under Printz the federal government can ask a state but can't order it, and the Elections Clause leaves the count to Washington's own procedures, so a list with nothing behind it but §611 can't pull ballots out.
fluid.text: Read the letter. It cites §611, gives no method and no evidence for any single person, and gives the state 24 hours. Whitehead's line, 'On this record, Defendants did not ask,' is the whole case: you can request cooperation, you can't threaten an official into setting votes aside.

coalition.zReason: The order holds the count steady through certification, but a 14-day TRO with an injunction hearing on Nov 18 isn't a final ruling, and the people celebrating it as one are setting themselves up.
coalition.text: I think the order is right, and the 62 people who never even got ballots tell you how sloppy that list was. But the people I vote with are treating a temporary restraining order like a final verdict and holding up the Elias lawyers as heroes. It's a TRO, the real fight is Nov 18, and DOJ can still investigate. I'd hold the applause.

denominated.zReason: The courts are the last thing standing between an authoritarian Justice Department and the ballots of eligible citizens, and this time they held.
denominated.text: An authoritarian DOJ tried to scare a state into throwing out citizens' votes, and a judge said no. That's the job.

fluid.zReason: The holding rests on Printz and the Elections Clause, both sound federalism, so it delivers the narrow point that DOJ can't commandeer Washington's count, even from a judge this station doesn't trust on much else.
fluid.text: Printz is a conservative precedent, and it fits here: Washington doesn't have to do DOJ's job because a U.S. Attorney held a press conference. The real failure was the letter, with no evidence, no method, and citizens on the list by the prosecutors' own admission. If Congress wants citizenship checked at the front door, that's what the SAVE Act is for, and it's sitting in the Senate.

coalition.zReason: The doctrine is fine, but the order leaves no working way to resolve suspect registrations before counties certify on Nov 24, so the check falls on prosecutions after the fact.
coalition.text: I hear people I vote with calling Whitehead 'a Biden judge,' and I get the frustration, but he's citing Printz, which is their doctrine too. What bothers me is that between this, California on Nov 2, and the Ninth Circuit, nobody in the system has a timely way to check a suspect registration before certification. Prosecuting someone in March doesn't take a vote back out of the count.

denominated.zReason: A Biden judge running an Elias Law Group lawsuit won't deliver an honest count; asking about citizenship has been turned into the offense.
denominated.text: A Biden judge, an Elias lawsuit, and now asking whether voters are citizens counts as intimidation. That's lawfare in a robe.

fluid.zReason: The order cuts off the aiding-and-abetting threats aimed at election workers and county auditors, and that's the pressure that could actually have gotten citizens' ballots pulled.
fluid.text: This was about working people. Naturalized grocery and meat workers in UFCW are exactly who a list of 'suspected noncitizens' sweeps up, and a federal prosecutor went on the radio talking about going to all 39 county auditors. Whitehead put it plainly: 'A threat of prosecution made for that purpose is not legal advice.' The county clerk doesn't have to choose between her job and somebody's vote anymore.

coalition.zReason: The order protects the count, but it leaves the list, the investigations and the prosecutions in place, so the people named on it are still exposed.
coalition.text: Sure, I'll take the win. But the people I organize with are cheering a federal judge and a big D.C. law firm like that settles it, and it doesn't. Those 400 names are still in DOJ's hands, they promised a second list, and the order says outright they can keep investigating. If you're a naturalized citizen on that list, a TRO doesn't make the knock on your door any less scary.

denominated.zReason: Courts and lawyers protect a process, not the people; DOJ keeps the list and the power to prosecute, so the targeting goes on.
denominated.text: A 14-day piece of paper doesn't take anybody's name off a government list. They'll come for immigrant voters some other way, and the courts will call it an investigation.

fluid.zReason: Setting those ballots aside until citizenship was settled was the only check that worked before certification, and the order removes it two days after the election, so suspect votes get counted first and questions come later.
fluid.text: Prosecutors flagged about 400 registered voters as possible noncitizens and asked for one thing: don't count those ballots until it's settled. Two days after the election, a judge says no, and counties certify on the 24th. You can prosecute somebody next year, but you can't pull their vote back out once it's certified. Where's the check?

coalition.zReason: The order still lets suspect ballots through before certification, but the list DOJ sent was weak enough that it handed the judge the case, so part of the failure sits with DOJ.
coalition.text: I want noncitizen voting stopped as much as anyone. But people I vote with are yelling 'rigged' about a list where 62 people never even got ballots and some had already shown citizenship papers at Licensing. If Serrano and Floyd had brought real evidence instead of §611 and a 24-hour deadline, this goes differently. Pass the SAVE Act and do it right.

denominated.zReason: A Biden judge working with the Elias machine won't let anyone check citizenship, so the count can't be trusted.
denominated.text: Rigged. A Biden judge and the Elias machine just made sure 400 suspect names stay in the count, no questions asked.
